strengths: Introduces EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA, a benchmark that uses SOTA action-recognition models (TIM/AVION) to mine hard distractors rather than relying on random sampling, humans, or closed-source LLMs, addressing a genuine gap in existing MQA-style video benchmarks that tend to have trivially easy distractors.

Comprehensive method suite (adversarial distractor training, egocentric prompting, vision-token supervision via an auxiliary action token, temporal start/end detection, GPT-4o distillation, direct prediction, and prior-action memory) is combined with systematic leave-one-out ablations that quantify each component's contribution.
Strong quantitative results: 21-point improvement over GPT-4o on the new hard benchmark and new SOTA accuracy on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 validation set using ground-truth narrations.

Demonstrates some generalization of the trained model to five of six additional action-related video benchmarks (EgoSchema, MVBench, VideoMME, LongVideoBench, PerceptionTest), suggesting the approach is not purely benchmark-specific overfitting.

Useful analysis contrasting 'official keys' vs. narrations as text targets, with both qualitative and quantitative evidence that compressed vocabulary labels introduce ambiguity that harms MLLM performance.
Reasonable reproducibility support: licensing table, full prompts for every auxiliary task, and training hyperparameters are disclosed in the appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely a recombination of existing techniques (hard-negative/adversarial mining, auxiliary token supervision, LLM distillation, temporal grounding) rather than a fundamentally new architectural or algorithmic idea; the contribution is more engineering/empirical than conceptual.

The benchmark's notion of 'hardness' is entirely defined by a single fixed action-recognition model's (TIM's) confidence rankings, which could bias the benchmark toward TIM's particular failure modes/biases rather than a more general or human-validated notion of distractor difficulty; no human verification of distractor plausibility is provided.

The 'learning prior actions' component uses ground-truth previous actions during training but only model predictions at test time, creating a train/test mismatch whose effect on real-world robustness (e.g., error propagation) is not analyzed.

Gains on the additional out-of-domain benchmarks (Table 5) are often small or even negative (e.g., -0.4 on NextQA, mixed/negative deltas across many VideoMME sub-categories in the appendix), which somewhat undercuts the claim of broad generalizability of the proposed training recipe.

The approach and benchmark are demonstrated only on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 (a single kitchen-domain egocentric dataset); it is unclear how well the MQA-construction methodology or the trained methods would transfer to other action domains (e.g., Ego4D, sports, general third-person video).

No variance/uncertainty reporting (single training runs) for the numerous ablations and comparisons, making it hard to assess whether the reported point differences (often <1-2 points) are statistically meaningful.

The scale of additional annotation (530K video-language pairs, GPT-4o distillation, multiple auxiliary tasks) introduces substantial data-engineering complexity, and the paper does not clearly disentangle how much of the improvement comes from this extra data/compute versus the specific proposed techniques.

strengths: Introduces a novel and scalable hard-example-mining approach (EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA) using SOTA specialist models (TIM, AVION) rather than humans or closed-source LLMs to generate difficult distractors, revealing substantial and interesting performance gaps in leading MLLMs including GPT-4o.

Extensive empirical validation: additive ablations, leave-one-out ablations, action-token design ablations, and an IID vs. OOD analysis (with JSD/statistical tests) supporting that gains are not simply from overfitting to a single distractor generator.

The two-stage structured action prediction pipeline is a practical and well-justified solution enabling fair, efficient comparison between MLLMs and specialized action recognition models (190x faster than a brute-force alternative), and the paper demonstrates SOTA on four separate action recognition benchmarks across different domains (cooking, tool assembly, animal behavior).

Broad evaluation across 13 general MLLM benchmarks (caption/open-ended/multi-choice) shows the model retains general video understanding while improving action-related sub-tasks, with detailed sub-category breakdowns provided in the appendix.
Reasonable interpretability analysis (attention correlation, action-token attention) offering some mechanistic support for the proposed action token design.
Strong reproducibility effort: detailed prompts, licensing table, training details, and code/data promised to be released.
weaknesses: Potential circularity/fairness concerns: the benchmark and much of the training data are built from distractors generated by the same class of specialist models (TIM/AVION) trained on the same underlying dataset, and although an OOD (AVION-train/TIM-test) setting is used, the two models may still share systematic biases inherited from the same dataset distribution.

The headline comparison against GPT-4o ("21 points") is conducted only at 8 frames due to API cost constraints, while LLaVAction's strongest reported numbers elsewhere use 16 or more frames; this limits the fairness/strength of the flagship claim.

Gains on the 13 general-purpose MLLM benchmarks (Table 7) are modest and mixed (several categories show LLaVAction underperforming the LLaVA-Video baseline, e.g., VideoMME, LongVideoBench subcategories), suggesting the benefits may be fairly narrow/domain-specific despite broad framing.

Ablations show the architectural novelty (action token) contributes a relatively modest improvement (~3.9 points) compared to data-centric changes (adversarial distractors, ~9.4 points), suggesting the primary contribution is largely a data curation strategy rather than a fundamentally new modeling technique.
The difficulty-level analysis (Table 8) relies on GPT-4o to rate its own/other models' distractor difficulty, raising potential circularity concerns for that specific analysis.

Limited diversity of base MLLMs used for the main results (mostly LLaVA-Video/LLaVA-OV variants); stronger or more recent open models (e.g., Qwen2-VL, InternVL) are only lightly tested (Animal Kingdom), leaving open whether findings generalize to other backbones.

Ethics statement is minimal and does not address dataset/domain biases (e.g., kitchen-only egocentric data, cultural representativeness) or potential surveillance/behavior-monitoring implications of fine-grained action recognition technology.
